module_title: Scaling Your Business: Contracts and Legalities

lessons.title: Understanding Basic Contract Terms
lessons.body:
A contract is a legally binding agreement between two or more parties. In Spanish, it's called a contrato. When you scale your business, you'll sign contracts with suppliers, clients, landlords, and employees. Knowing key terms helps you avoid costly mistakes. 

First, parties: las partes. The offeror is el oferente, and the offeree is el aceptante. Consideration (something of value exchanged) is la contraprestaciÃ³n. For example, if you agree to buy 100 kg of cocoa from a farmer in Ghana for 500 cedis, that's a contract. 

Key clauses: 
- Objeto del contrato: purpose of the contract. 
- Plazo: term or duration. 
- Precio: price. 
- Forma de pago: payment method. 
- ClÃ¡usula de rescisiÃ³n: termination clause. 
- PenalizaciÃ³n por incumplimiento: penalty for breach. 

In many African countries, oral contracts are valid, but written contracts are safer. For cross-border deals, specify jurisdiction (jurisdicciÃ³n) and arbitration (arbitraje). For instance, 'Las partes acuerdan resolver disputas mediante arbitraje en la CÃ¡mara de Comercio de Nairobi.' 

Always check for a 'clÃ¡usula de fuerza mayor' (force majeure) to protect against unforeseen events like floods or strikes. Also, ensure both parties sign and date (firma y fecha) the document. Keep copies. If you don't understand a term, ask a lawyer or use a translation tool like DeepL. 

Practice: Write a simple contract in Spanish for a service you offer. Use at least five terms from above. This builds your vocabulary and confidence.

lessons.title: Discussing Terms and Conditions
lessons.body:
Terms and conditions (tÃ©rminos y condiciones) are the rules of your contract. When negotiating, you'll discuss these in Spanish. Start with 'Quisiera negociar los tÃ©rminos' (I would like to negotiate the terms). 

Common phrases: 
- 'Â¿EstÃ¡ de acuerdo con estas condiciones?' (Do you agree with these conditions?) 
- 'Propongo un pago del 50% por adelantado.' (I propose a 50% advance payment.) 
- 'Â¿Podemos incluir una clÃ¡usula de confidencialidad?' (Can we include a confidentiality clause?) 
- 'El plazo de entrega serÃ¡ de 30 dÃ­as.' (The delivery term will be 30 days.) 
- 'Si hay retraso, se aplicarÃ¡ una multa del 2% por semana.' (If there is a delay, a 2% penalty per week will apply.) 

In Africa, business relationships often rely on trust, but clear terms prevent disputes. For example, a Kenyan supplier might agree to deliver goods in 45 days, but if you don't specify, delays can hurt your cash flow. Always clarify: 'Â¿QuÃ© sucede si no se cumple el plazo?' (What happens if the deadline is not met?) 

Use tools like Google Translate for quick checks, but for legal documents, hire a translator. In Spanish-speaking countries like Equatorial Guinea, contracts are in Spanish, so knowing these phrases is essential. 

Practice role-play: One person is the buyer, the other the seller. Negotiate payment terms, delivery, and penalties. Record yourself and listen for accuracy. This will prepare you for real negotiations.

lessons.title: Registering a Business: Vocabulary and Phrases
lessons.body:
To scale legally, you must register your business. In Spanish, registration is 'registro de empresa' or 'constituciÃ³n de sociedad'. Common business structures: 
- Empresa unipersonal (sole proprietorship) 
- Sociedad de responsabilidad limitada (S.R.L. or LLC) 
- Sociedad anÃ³nima (S.A. or corporation) 

Steps to register in a Spanish-speaking country (e.g., Equatorial Guinea or Spain): 
1. Reserva de nombre (name reservation) at the commercial registry. 
2. Escritura pÃºblica (public deed) before a notary. 
3. NÃºmero de IdentificaciÃ³n Fiscal (NIF) or tax ID. 
4. Registro Mercantil (Commercial Registry). 
5. Licencia de apertura (opening license) from the municipality. 

Key phrases: 
- 'Quiero registrar una sociedad de responsabilidad limitada.' (I want to register a limited liability company.) 
- 'Â¿CuÃ¡les son los requisitos?' (What are the requirements?) 
- 'Necesito el formulario de solicitud.' (I need the application form.) 
- 'Â¿CuÃ¡nto cuesta la inscripciÃ³n?' (How much does registration cost?) 

In many African countries, you can register online. For example, in Nigeria, the CAC (Corporate Affairs Commission) allows online registration. In Spanish-speaking countries, the process may take 1-2 weeks and cost between $200 and $1000. 

After registration, you'll get a Tax ID (NIF) and must file annual returns. Keep your registration documents safe. If you expand to another country, you may need to register a branch (sucursal). 

Practice: Look up the registration process for a Spanish-speaking country you're interested in. Write a short paragraph in Spanish describing the steps.

lessons.title: Taxes and Licenses in Spanish-Speaking Countries
lessons.body:
Taxes (impuestos) and licenses (licencias) are mandatory for scaling. In Spanish-speaking countries, common taxes include: 
- IVA (Impuesto al Valor Agregado): VAT, typically 15-21%. 
- Impuesto sobre la Renta (ISR): income tax, 25-35%. 
- Impuesto de Sociedades: corporate tax. 

You must also get licenses: licencia de funcionamiento (operating license), licencia sanitaria (health license) for food businesses, and licencia ambiental (environmental license). 

Key phrases: 
- 'Â¿DÃ³nde puedo pagar los impuestos?' (Where can I pay taxes?) 
- 'Necesito una licencia de funcionamiento.' (I need an operating license.) 
- 'Â¿CuÃ¡l es la fecha lÃ­mite para declarar impuestos?' (What is the deadline to file taxes?) 
- 'Â¿Hay exenciones para pequeÃ±as empresas?' (Are there exemptions for small businesses?) 

In Equatorial Guinea, the tax authority is 'DirecciÃ³n General de Impuestos'. In Spain, it's 'Agencia Tributaria'. In many African countries, tax rates are lower for small businesses. For example, in Kenya, small businesses with turnover below 5 million KES pay a presumptive tax. 

Always keep receipts (recibos) and invoices (facturas). Use accounting software like QuickBooks or Wave. If you're late, you may face multas (fines) and interest (intereses). 

Consider hiring an accountant (contador) to handle taxes. They cost around $100-$300 per month but save you from penalties. 

Practice: List three taxes your business would pay in a Spanish-speaking country. Write a sentence in Spanish about each.

lessons.title: Hiring Employees and Writing Job Descriptions
lessons.body:
Hiring (contrataciÃ³n) is key to scaling. In Spanish, an employee is 'empleado' and a job description is 'descripciÃ³n del puesto'. 

A job description should include: 
- TÃ­tulo del puesto (job title) 
- Funciones (duties) 
- Requisitos (requirements) 
- Salario (salary) 
- Horario (schedule) 
- UbicaciÃ³n (location) 

Example: 'Buscamos un vendedor con experiencia en ventas de productos agrÃ­colas. Debe hablar espaÃ±ol e inglÃ©s. Salario: 300.000 CFA por mes.' 

When interviewing, ask: 
- 'Â¿CuÃ¡l es su experiencia previa?' (What is your previous experience?) 
- 'Â¿Por quÃ© quiere trabajar aquÃ­?' (Why do you want to work here?) 
- 'Â¿Puede trabajar los fines de semana?' (Can you work weekends?) 

In many African countries, labor laws require written contracts (contrato de trabajo), minimum wage (salario mÃ­nimo), and social security (seguridad social). For example, in Senegal, the minimum wage is about 333 CFA per hour. In Equatorial Guinea, it's 150,000 CFA per month. 

You must also register employees for social security and pay contributions. Failure can lead to fines. 

Use platforms like LinkedIn or local job boards to post openings. For Spanish-speaking roles, specify 'Se requiere espaÃ±ol fluido'. 

Practice: Write a job description in Spanish for a position in your business. Include at least five details.

lessons.body:
Now, let's review a simple contract in Spanish. Below is a short service contract. Read it and answer the questions.

Questions:

Answers: 1. DiseÃ±ar un logotipo. 2. 200.000 CFA. 3. 15 dÃ­as. 4. 50% adelantado, 50% al final. 5. Se puede rescindir con 7 dÃ­as de aviso. 

Now, practice with a contract from your own business. Identify key terms and translate them. Use a dictionary if needed. This exercise builds your confidence to handle real contracts in Spanish.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Scaling Your Business â Contracts and Legalities in Spanish-Speaking Markets

For African agribusinesses expanding into Spanish-speaking markets â whether exporting cocoa from Ghana to Colombia, supplying sesame from Ethiopia to Mexico, or partnering with cooperatives in Peru â the ability to read, negotiate, and register contracts in Spanish is not a "nice-to-have." It is a commercial survival skill. This Practical Reference module consolidates the six lessons in this unit into one operational toolkit: contract vocabulary, terms-and-conditions negotiation phrases, business registration language, tax and licensing terminology, hiring and job-description wording, and a structured method for reviewing a simple contract in Spanish.

The approach is business-first. Every term below is framed around what it protects, what it costs, and what it commits your enterprise to. Where a phrase is legally loaded â meaning it can shift liability, delay payment, or trigger penalties â it is flagged.

Lesson 1 â Understanding Basic Contract Terms

A Spanish-language contract for agricultural goods typically opens with las partes (the parties), el objeto (the subject matter), and la contraprestaciÃ³n (the consideration). The most dangerous words for an African exporter are often the smallest: solidaria means joint and several liability, so if your buyer defaults, the guarantor can be pursued for the full amount. Irrevocable means you cannot withdraw. Salvo buen fin means "subject to final collection" â a clause that lets a buyer's bank reverse a credit if the underlying documents fail.

Key contract vocabulary you will meet repeatedly: el contrato de compraventa (sales contract), el proveedor (supplier), el comprador (buyer), la clÃ¡usula (clause), el anexo (annex), la vigencia (term/validity), la penalidad (penalty), and la rescisiÃ³n (termination). In agribusiness, la merma (shrinkage/wastage) and el calibre (size grade) are commercially decisive â a one-point change in calibre can swing the price per tonne by 8â12%.

Lesson 2 â Discussing Terms and Conditions

Negotiation phrases that actually move a deal: QuisiÃ©ramos proponer una modificaciÃ³n a la clÃ¡usula de pago (We would like to propose an amendment to the payment clause). Â¿PodrÃ­an ampliar el plazo de pago a 60 dÃ­as? (Could you extend the payment term to 60 days?). Proponemos que la jurisdicciÃ³n sea la CÃ¡mara de Comercio de Lima (We propose jurisdiction be the Lima Chamber of Commerce).

The table below maps common Spanish contract clauses to their commercial effect on an African agribusiness.

Table 1: Contract clauses and their commercial impact
Spanish term English meaning Commercial impact on your business
AnticipoAdvance payment / depositImproves cash flow; typically 10â30% for first-time suppliers.
Plazo de pagoPayment term30/60/90 days. 90 days can cripple a small exporter's working capital.
InterÃ©s moratorioLate-payment interestYour only leverage if the buyer delays. Insist on 1â2% monthly.
Fuerza mayorForce majeureProtects both sides against drought, strikes, port closure.
ArbitrajeArbitrationFaster and cheaper than court; specify seat and language.
ConfidencialidadConfidentialityProtects your buyer list, pricing, and processing methods.
Penalidad por incumplimientoBreach penaltyCap it â uncapped penalties can exceed contract value.
Cesion de contratoAssignmentIf unregulated, your buyer can sell the contract to a third party.

Source: ITC Model Contracts for Small Firms and UNCTAD contract negotiation resources.

Lesson 3 â Registering a Business: Vocabulary and Phrases

Registration terminology varies by country, but the core vocabulary is stable. In Mexico you register before the Registro PÃºblico de Comercio and obtain an RFC. In Colombia it is the CÃ¡mara de Comercio and RUT. In Peru it is SUNARP and RUC. In Spain it is the Registro Mercantil and NIF/CIF. Common phrases: Constituir una sociedad (to incorporate a company), Escritura pÃºblica (notarised deed), Objeto social (corporate purpose â keep it broad enough to cover future agri-processing), Capital social (share capital), and Representante legal (legal representative).

For an African agribusiness, the practical question is usually whether to register a local subsidiary or work through a local agent. A subsidiary gives you personerÃ­a jurÃ­dica (legal personality) and access to local credit, but exposes you to local corporate tax. An agent is faster and cheaper but leaves you without standing to enforce contracts in your own name.

Lesson 4 â Taxes and Licenses in Spanish-Speaking Countries

Tax acronyms differ across the region: IVA (Impuesto al Valor Agregado) in most countries, IGV in Peru, ITBMS in Panama. Corporate income tax is Impuesto sobre la Renta (ISR) or Impuesto a la Renta. Exporters frequently qualify for devoluciÃ³n de IVA (VAT refund) or drawback, but only if the paperwork is exact. Licences you will encounter include licencia de funcionamiento (operating licence), permiso sanitario (health permit, critical for food exports), and certificado fitosanitario (phytosanitary certificate, issued by the national plant-protection authority).

Table 2: Tax and licence terminology by country

Source: OECD Revenue Statistics in Latin America and the Caribbean; national tax authority portals (SAT, DIAN, SUNAT, SII, AEAT, DGI).

Lesson 5 â Hiring Employees and Writing Job Descriptions

Hiring in Spanish-speaking markets requires familiarity with el contrato de trabajo (employment contract), el periodo de prueba (probation period â usually 1â3 months), la jornada laboral (working hours), el salario mÃ­nimo (minimum wage), and las prestaciones sociales (mandatory benefits: health, pension, severance). In many countries, aguinaldo (Christmas bonus) and prima vacacional (vacation premium) are legally required and must be budgeted before you sign.

A job description in Spanish should include: tÃ­tulo del puesto (job title), objetivo del puesto (role objective), responsabilidades (responsibilities), requisitos (requirements), competencias (skills), and condiciones (conditions). For agribusiness roles such as tÃ©cnico de campo (field technician), supervisor de planta (plant supervisor), or gerente de exportaciones (export manager), specify the crop, the region, and the reporting line â vague descriptions invite disputes.

â  SAFETY WARNING â Legal and Financial Risk

Never sign a Spanish-language contract you have not had reviewed by a qualified local lawyer. Machine translation is not sufficient for clauses involving jurisdicciÃ³n, arbitraje, penalidad, or solidaridad. A single mistranslated clause â for example, treating solidaria as "shared" rather than "joint and several" â can expose your entire enterprise to liability far exceeding the contract value. Also verify that your counterparty's NIT/RUC/RFC is active before signing; a cancelled tax ID means the contract may be unenforceable.

Lesson 6 â Practice: Review a Simple Contract in Spanish

Take any short Spanish sales contract and run it through the five-stage workflow in the diagram above. For each stage, write one sentence in Spanish summarising what the contract says, and one sentence in English stating whether you accept it. This dual-language discipline forces precision and creates a record you can share with your lawyer.

Example: "El vendedor entregarÃ¡ 20 toneladas de cafÃ© verde, calibre 15, en el puerto de Buenaventura dentro de 30 dÃ­as." Your review note: "Delivery: 20 t green coffee, grade 15, Buenaventura port, 30 days. Accept â but confirm who bears port storage if the vessel is delayed."

Quick Reference Checklist

  1. Identify all parties â verify razÃ³n social and tax ID (NIT/RUC/RFC) are active.
  2. Confirm the object â product, grade (calibre), quantity, and Incoterm are unambiguous.
  3. Check payment terms â anticipo, plazo de pago, and interÃ©s moratorio are stated numerically.
  4. Review liability â watch for solidaria, uncapped penalidad, and salvo buen fin.
  5. Agree jurisdiction â arbitraje seat, language, and ley aplicable are specified.
  6. Verify licences â permiso sanitario and certificado fitosanitario are valid and current.
  7. Budget employment costs â prestaciones sociales, aguinaldo, and prima vacacional included.
  8. Archive everything â signed copy, translations, and correspondence stored digitally for five years.

Further Reading (Free Official Sources)

  • International Trade Centre â Model Contracts for Small Firms
  • UNCTAD â Competition and Consumer Protection Resources
  • OECD â Revenue Statistics in Latin America and the Caribbean
  • WIPO â Contracts and IP for SMEs
  • FAOLEX â National Agri-Food Legislation Database

This module is a practical language and business reference, not legal advice. Always engage a qualified local lawyer before signing or registering.
